chapters.title: The Annihilation of Beni
paragraphs: Beni-Sanghar
One

It was morning. Byomkesh sat in his Keyatala house with a cup of tea and the newspaper. It was a winter morning, around eight o’clock. I, Ajit, had already hurriedly finished my tea and gone out—there was a meeting to be had with a famous author. The gentleman had promised to give me a copy of his new book, but celebrated writers have many suitors; it was necessary to secure the book in advance.

After finishing the advertisements in the newspaper, Byomkesh lifted his teacup. The remaining tea had grown cold; with a single gulp he emptied the cup and picked up the paper again. Now it was time to read the news.

These days, reading the newspaper makes it clear that the world is not in its right mind. Earthquakes, tidal waves, floods, droughts—these are ever-present, but beyond that, people themselves seem to have gone mad. War, revolution, internal strife, strikes, lockouts, bombs, tear gas, lathi charges. Perhaps it is because the population has grown so vast that no one finds peace anymore. Where there is such crowding and congestion, how can peace be found?

He did not need to turn the page. On the very first page was the account of a dreadful murder. The killing had occurred the night before last, was discovered yesterday morning, and today it was in the paper. It had happened in South Calcutta, not far from Byomkesh’s own home; a short walk south along the main road brought one to the immense three-storied house, with the name “Benimadhab” inscribed in large letters across its forehead. Byomkesh had passed by the house many times, but had never made the acquaintance of its inhabitants. From the newspaper he learned that the owner, the elderly Benimadhab Chakraborty, and his bodyguard had both been murdered in a brutal fashion.

Byomkesh read the account of the murder with keen attention, then absentmindedly lit a cigarette. Such a ghastly crime had taken place in the neighborhood the night before last, and yet he had heard nothing of it. Rakhal was the local inspector; surely he had taken charge of the investigation, but had not informed Byomkesh. Perhaps the matter was straightforward, with no mystery or complexity, and so Rakhal had not come. These days, even a truly intricate mystery had become a rare thing—
The telephone rang. Byomkesh reached out and held the receiver to his ear. From the other end came a voice: “Byomkesh-da? It’s Rakhal. Have you read today’s paper?”
Byomkesh replied, “I have. Beni-Sanghar?”
“What did you say—Beni-Sanghar? Oh yes, yes, Beni-Sanghar indeed, along with Meghraj-badh. I’m speaking from the scene itself.”
“What’s the matter?”
“The matter seems a bit tangled. I’ve been investigating since yesterday morning. Still no—”

No trace could be found. Are you very busy?' 'No.' 'Then could you come over here once? It’s not far from your house, just five minutes away. The house is called Benimadhab.' 'I know it.' 'When will you come?' 'Immediately.'
Two

Benimadhab Chakraborty had amassed a fortune as a contractor for the government’s military department. His sprawling three-storied house on Sadar Road in South Calcutta was but a modest testament to that wealth.

Benimadhab was a man of shrewd intelligence. Years of contracting had stripped him of faith in the honesty of mankind. Yet, for all that, his heart had not grown narrow. He accepted the faults of his family—and his own—with a smile.

Benimadhab’s household was not large. He had become a widower soon after reaching manhood; his wife left behind a son and a daughter. When they came of age, Benimadhab arranged their marriages. The son, Ajay, grew into a thorough good-for-nothing; after squandering some of his father’s money in failed business ventures, he returned to rest on his father’s shoulders. Benimadhab made no further attempt to employ him. He himself spent most of his time away from home; Ajay lived on the second floor with his wife Arati and their children, Makaranda and Laboni. Benimadhab provided for their household expenses.

He had married off his daughter well; his son-in-law, Gangadhar, had inherited property. But, emboldened by his wealthy father-in-law, Gangadhar lost everything at the races. His daughter, Gayatri, returned to her father in tears. Benimadhab took in his daughter, son-in-law, and granddaughter Jhillika; just as he gave his son a monthly allowance, he allotted the same for his daughter.

Benimadhab’s house, as I have said, was three stories high. The top floor had only three rooms, the rest was a vast terrace. Benimadhab kept this floor for himself; if he was away, it remained locked. The second floor had eight rooms and a continuous veranda in front; here, Benimadhab arranged for his son Ajay and daughter Gayatri to live side by side. Their kitchens, of course, were separate. There was no harmony between the two households, but neither dared quarrel openly. Benimadhab was fond of his children, but he was a man of gravity, and knew how to be strict.

On the ground floor was a massive hall, furnished in the English style like a drawing-room: a low round table in the center, two sofas and several heavy, cushioned chairs around it, and a few more stiff-backed chairs lined up against the wall. But the room was rarely used; only on the rare occasion when a visitor called would a guest be seated there. The remaining five rooms, though designated for guests and visitors, were locked up most of the time.
But they did not remain locked for long. Benimadhab had two younger maternal cousins, both long since deceased...
Beni Sanhar

...had gone; their two sons, Sanat Ganguli and Nikhil Haldar—cousins by their mothers—worked in Calcutta. They did not have good lodgings, so Benimadhab brought them into his own house. They stayed in two rooms on the ground floor.

So it appears: Benimadhab’s sons, daughters, grandchildren, and two nephews—seven dependents in all. There were no male servants in the house; two maids came during the day to do the chores and left by evening. The atmosphere was utterly monotonous. The brothers-in-law were of almost the same age, forty-three and forty-four; but there was no real intimacy between them, and their personalities were quite different. Ajay was handsome and something of a dandy; he never stepped out of the house without a starched dhuti-panjabi and polished pump shoes. He strongly objected to going to the Gariahat market every morning; most days, his wife Arati went instead. Ajay went to the club in the evenings; he had a deep passion for amateur theatre. He enjoyed acting. The club itself was for amateur dramatics—they staged four or five plays every year.

Gangadhar’s appearance was almost ascetic; his face and body were lean, more bone than flesh. His gaze was sharp. Having squandered his own property and come to live off his father-in-law, he had become extremely grave and taciturn. He never left the house during the day; after dusk, he would go out for a walk with a stick in hand. When he returned an hour or so later, the smell of liquor would waft from his mouth.

Between the sisters-in-law, there was a surface cordiality—visits and gossip—but given the chance, neither would hesitate to take a swipe at the other. Gayatri might go to the next flat and say, “Boudi, what have you cooked today?”
Arati would recite her menu and ask, “And what did you cook, dear?”

Gayatri replied, “What cooking! I was about to put the meat on after draining the rice water, when I found there was no garam masala! You know your brother-in-law can’t eat just greens and rice. He can do without fish, but he must have meat every day. So I came to check if you had any garam masala in your pantry. Otherwise, I’ll have to send the maid to the market again.”
Arati said, “Of course I have some, here you go.”
Handing over the garam masala, Arati smiled and said, “There’s nothing wrong with Nandai loving meat, but honestly, he could do without that other thing.”
Gayatri’s gaze hardened at once. “What thing?”

Arati put on her most innocent face. “Your brother was saying the other evening he ran into Nandai, and there was a strong smell of liquor on his breath. Maybe it’s an old habit he can’t shake, but if Father hears of it—”

Gayatri’s hard gaze turned sly, and with a crooked smile she said, “If Father hears of it, it’ll be because you tell him, Boudi. But would that be wise? You keep a dance master for your daughter, nothing wrong with that, but is it right for Laboni to go out to the cinema with the master till midnight? Laboni’s no little girl—if she gets into some scandal, will Father be pleased?” With a swirl of her sari end, Gayatri left.
Tit for tat, embrace for embrace.

Laboni was a pretty girl; slender and tall, her figure suited for dance. She was a bit restless by nature, her schooling had ended before she finished the upper grades, and she had a wild passion for dance. Seeing his daughter’s inclination, Ajay had arranged for a dance master for her. The master was a young man from a respectable family, named Parag Laha; twice a week he came to teach Laboni dance...
Byomkesh Samagra

Lavani would practice her dance right before her parents’ eyes. Occasionally, Parag would say, “A new foreign film on dance and music is playing. I’ve bought two tickets for the night show. Shall I take Lavani? She could learn a lot from it.”
At first, Arati would refuse. Parag would reply, “Very well, I’ll take another student instead.”
Gradually, her objections softened. Lavani began going to the cinema with Parag; late at night, Parag would escort her home.
With time, everything becomes familiar, even the unusual.

Lavani’s elder brother Makrand was enrolled in college. But his studies were nominal; his name was on the rolls, nothing more. His horizon was filled with political squabbles, and he only set foot in college when party affairs demanded it. He was good-looking, but his face and eyes bore a fierce, hungry dissatisfaction. He rarely stayed at home; his connection to the household was limited to meals and sleep. From time to time, money for Arati’s household expenses would vanish; Arati understood who had taken it, but remained silent for fear of discord. Makrand harbored a deep resentment for his theatre-loving father, and Ajay too disapproved of his son’s ways; the two avoided each other, as if Makrand were an unwelcome guest in his own parents’ home.

In the adjacent flat lived a small family: only a daughter, Jhilli. Jhilli was Lavani’s age, not as beautiful, but much better at her studies. She was a reserved girl, newly admitted to college, attending classes regularly, diligent in her work, and helping her mother with household chores whenever she could. Her calm face betrayed nothing of her inner world.
Such was the general state of affairs on the second floor.

Downstairs, in two rooms, lived Sanat and Nikhil. Sanat was over thirty; Nikhil, under thirty. Both could be called men of presence, but their characters were entirely different. Sanat was reserved and taciturn, never speaking without thought. Nikhil, on the other hand, was quick-tongued, lively, and fond of jest. Both worked as journalists. Sanat was a press photographer. Nikhil worked as a junior news editor in the editorial department of a newspaper. He was a nocturnal creature—“When the gods sleep, our day begins; when the gods wake, our night falls.” They were kin to those who once tempted Rishyashringa.

Neither had married. Nikhil’s reason was simple: his earnings were insufficient to support a household. Sanat, however, had no such excuse. He earned well; his reason for living in his maternal uncle’s house was not lack of means, but lack of a suitable home. To seek the root of his aversion to marriage, one would have to consult a secret album. In that album were many lively photographs of enchanting young women. Seeing those pictures, one might suspect that, though Sanat was unmarried, he was no celibate. Yet he was an exceedingly cautious man. If, instead of marriage, he had adopted the ways of a honeybee, it was all done without anyone’s knowledge.

These seven people were the permanent residents of the house. Benimadhab would come once or twice a year, stay for a couple of days, and then return to Delhi. Delhi was the center of his professional world.

Suddenly, at the age of sixty-seven, Benimadhab’s health broke down. He had always been robust, capable of tremendous exertion. But after the death of his beloved servant and long-time companion, Rambhajan, he could not remain upright for long. Within three months, he wound up his business. He had no need for money; he had worked out of sheer habit, right up to old age. Now, closing his Delhi office, he returned to Calcutta. With him came a new...
Beni Sanghar

The servant Meghraj. After the death of Rambhajan, Benimadhab kept Meghraj as his personal attendant. Meghraj had once been a sepoy in the Indian Army; during the Sino-Indian war, he was wounded and lost a leg up to the knee. The Indian Army provided him with an artificial limb and discharged him with a modest pension. He managed to secure a job as a doorman at Benimadhab’s Delhi office, which put bread on his table; after Rambhajan’s death, Benimadhab brought him on as his personal servant. Meghraj was a man of utmost loyalty and a strict disposition; he took charge of all the affairs of Benimadhab’s solitary household, from shaving his master’s beard to polishing his shoes. He was about forty, with a robust build. Because of the artificial leg, he walked with a slight limp.

Thus, Benimadhab came and settled in his Calcutta house. The upper floor had all the necessary amenities for daily life, except for a fridge and a telephone. Within a few days, both fridge and telephone were installed. In the meantime, his daughter Gayatri came with a request—“Baba, this time let me take care of your meals. Earlier, whenever you came, you would eat at Dada’s place. Are we nobody to you?”
Benimadhab replied, “But I am not alone—Meghraj is here.”
“Is Meghraj the name of your new servant? Ah, poor old Rambhajan is gone. Well, I’ll feed Meghraj too.”
After some thought, Benimadhab said, “Very well, but that will increase your expenses. I’m raising your monthly allowance by another hundred and fifty rupees.”
Gayatri laughed and said, “As you wish.” Perhaps this was her intention all along; she used to receive seven hundred and fifty rupees a month, now it stood at nine hundred.

No sooner had he arrived in Calcutta than Benimadhab summoned his old friend, Dr. Abinash Sen. Dr. Abinash Sen was a renowned physician, a few years younger than Benimadhab. One day, he took Benimadhab to his clinic and conducted a thorough examination—X-rays, ECG, and other mechanical tests. Then Dr. Sen said, “Look, you have no serious illness; what you are experiencing is simply the natural, all-encompassing decline of old age. I won’t prescribe you any medicines, only a monthly injection to keep your glands invigorated. The truth is, you have worked far too hard for your age. From now on, complete rest: read books, listen to the radio, take a stroll every evening.”
Benimadhab received the injection and returned home in good spirits.

And so the days passed. Gayatri would arrange his plate herself and feed her father. The others came and went. Makaranda rarely visited, and even when he did, he stayed only a couple of minutes. The granddaughters stayed, chatting with Benimadhab; the old man was pleased to hear that Jhillie was doing well in her studies, and he was not displeased to learn that Laboni was learning to dance. Though advanced in years, he was not old-fashioned. When every girl is learning to dance, why shouldn’t his granddaughter?

Some twenty or twenty-five days went by, and then, quite suddenly, Benimadhab fell ill—dysentery, abdominal pain. Dr. Sen came, examined him, and said, “You’ve overindulged in food; you must be careful with your diet.”
Everyone in the house was present. Gayatri said with a long face, “But Doctor, I haven’t given Baba anything to eat that could have made him ill.”
The doctor said nothing, merely wrote out a prescription and dietary instructions, and took his leave.
He paused—“I’ll call and check on you from time to time.”
After the doctor left, Benimadhab turned to Arati and said, “Daughter-in-law, I leave the responsibility of preparing my diet to you.”
Arati, suppressing her triumph, replied, “Yes, Father.”
Within three or four days, Benimadhab recovered; his stomach settled. He abandoned his bland diet and began eating regular food. Arati continued to cook for him.

But Benimadhab’s mind was not at peace. All his life he had spent his days in the company of various people, engaged in various pursuits; now, his life was stripped of all variety. In the morning, Meghraj shaved his beard, he bathed, had his tea, and sat down with the newspaper. That occupied him for about an hour. Then he would turn on the radio and listen to music for a while. The music didn’t please him for long; he would switch off the radio and leaf through books and magazines.

One day, memories of old friends in Calcutta surfaced. He searched the telephone directory for their names, called some and reached a few, others not; for a while, they reminisced about the old days. After eleven, Arati would arrive with his plate of rice. After the meal, he would spend an hour lying on his bed, dozing in the afternoon.
In the evening, Jhilli or Laboni would come, and he would chat with them for a while. He would say to Laboni, “Let’s see how well you’ve learned to dance.”
Laboni would reply, “I haven’t learned well yet, Grandpa. When I do, I’ll show you.”
Benimadhab would ask, “Is your teacher any good?”
Laboni, flushed with excitement, would say, “Very good. So good that—” Embarrassed, she would stop midway.
Benimadhab would ask, “How old is your teacher?”
“How should I know! Must be twenty-six or twenty-seven. I have to go, Mother’s calling.” Laboni would hurry away.

After sunset, Benimadhab would pace the open terrace for a long time. Sometimes he wished to go to Rabindra Sarobar, to stroll among people for a while; but climbing three flights of stairs was too much for him, so his exercise was limited to the rooftop.

At nine at night, after finishing his meal, he would retire to bed. Such was his daily routine. Meghraj was always close at hand; sometimes inside the room, sometimes just outside the door. Once Benimadhab lay down, Meghraj would go downstairs, eat his dinner, then return, gently close Benimadhab’s door, and spread his bedding outside, standing guard through the night.

Thus the days passed. One day, after a telephone conversation with a professor friend, Benimadhab’s face grew grave. He set down the receiver and sat thinking for a while, then called Meghraj and said, “Go downstairs and fetch Makrand.”

A few minutes later, Makrand appeared. Summoned by the servant, he was not pleased; his face bore a look of displeasure as he gazed at his grandfather, question in his eyes. Benimadhab regarded his tall, robust figure for a while, then asked, “You’ve started college—how are your studies going?”
Makrand’s face darkened with a deep frown. “They’re going, more or less.”
Benimadhab said, “I’ve heard you don’t attend classes, that you roam about in a gang doing politics. Is that true?”
Makrand replied insolently, “Who told you that?”
Benimadhab said sharply, “Who told me is none of your concern. Is it true or not?”
Beni Sanhar 931
“Yes, it’s true.” Makrand’s eyes reddened as he stared at his grandfather.
“Indeed!” Sparks of anger flashed in Benimadhab’s eyes as well. “You have learned insolence. —Meghraj!”

Meghraj had been standing outside the door; he entered the room. Benimadhab pointed a finger and commanded, “Grab this boy by the ear, slap him across the face, and then throw him out by the scruff of his neck.”

Meghraj had once been a sepoy; he was a servant of orders. As instructed, he seized Makrand by the ear and struck him on the cheek. However much impudence Makrand harbored in his heart, he lacked both the courage and the physical strength to grapple with Meghraj. Stumbling from the blow, he was pushed out of the room.

The matter could no longer be concealed. Ajay and Arati rushed in and begged Benimadhab’s forgiveness. Benimadhab remained grave, and at last said, “There is but one boy in the family, and he has grown wild and insolent. The fault is yours—you do not know how to discipline a child.”
The affair did not escalate further.

Then, one afternoon, Sanat came to visit his uncle. Sanat and Nikhil would sometimes come and sit with their uncle, inquire after his well-being with due respect, and then depart. Today, Sanat had brought his camera, and said, “Uncle, I’d like to take your photograph.”
Benimadhab smiled and replied, “I am an old man—what use is there in taking my picture?”
Sanat said, “I’ll keep it in my album.”
“But the light is fading now; can you take a picture in this light?”
“I can. I’ve brought a flash bulb.”
“Very well, go ahead.” Benimadhab settled into a leaning chair.

Sanat was preparing to take the photograph when Nikhil entered. Sanat moved about, searching for the right angle, and at last took the picture from a particular vantage; the bulb flashed once and went out.
Nikhil said, “Sanatda, when the photograph is ready, give me a copy. I’ll print it in the paper. Uncle has retired from work and settled in Calcutta; the news should be published.”
Benimadhab was inwardly pleased with his nephews.

The next day, Sanat brought the photograph to show Benimadhab. The picture had come out well; Benimadhab’s age-worn face, through the artist’s skill, had acquired a gentle and serene expression. There was no doubt that Sanat was a deft artist.
Benimadhab said, “It’s very good. If you have it framed and hung somewhere, that will do.”
Sanat replied, “I’ll enlarge it, frame it, and bring it over. I’ve given Nikhil a copy—he’ll print it in the paper.”

And so, Benimadhab’s idle, languid days passed. Sanat had the large photograph framed and hung it on the wall of the room. His picture and a brief introduction appeared in the newspaper. In such circumstances, a man in his old age should find peace and comfort. But peace and comfort did not come to Benimadhab’s heart. He could not enjoy continuous closeness with the families of his son and daughter. “Perhaps this is what happens to those who, forgetting the taste of family life, have walked alone for so many years.”

On the other hand, there was no happiness in his son’s or daughter’s families either. Gayatri’s temper was always irritable. Gangadhar spent his days sitting alone, playing solitaire; at dusk he would slip out quietly, only to return before it grew too late. Ajay would once spend many late nights at the club, lost in adda or rehearsals; this had been his chief indulgence in life. Now he was required to return home by nine o’clock, for the master’s order was that after nine, the main door would remain closed.

No. If he returned home after nine and pushed at the door, the sound would carry up to the third floor, and that was not desirable. Everyone kept an eye and an ear alert toward the third floor. Even though Arati was always trying to please her father-in-law, she could not be at ease.

Only two girls on the second floor, Laboni and Jhilli, and Sanat and Nikhil on the ground floor, were truly at ease. Jhilli and Laboni were only eighteen; their sense of the world was not yet mature. The situation was different for Sanat and Nikhil; their uncle had indeed allowed them to stay in his house, but they had no expectations of money from him. There was no possibility that Benimadhab would learn of Sanat’s secret nocturnal excursions. Nikhil was not guilty of such things; moreover, for the past few months, he had been absorbed in something new.

One day, before Benimadhab had settled in Calcutta, Nikhil suddenly received a letter by post, an envelope. There was no one who would write to him, so he was a little surprised as he opened it. On a single sheet of paper, just two lines were written—
I am a girl. I love you.—
There was no name beneath the letter.
Nikhil stared at it like a fool for a while. Then a delighted smile spread across his face. A girl loved him! Well, well! What a joke!
But who was the girl?

Nikhil examined the postmark on the envelope; the seal was smudged, but it was clear the letter had been posted in Calcutta. A girl from Calcutta. Who could it be? And why write a letter? There were so many easier ways to confess love. Was she too shy to say it aloud, so she wrote instead? But why not sign her name?

Nikhil knew many girls. There were at least ten unmarried women working in his office. Besides, there were his friends’ sisters. The girls were fond of him for his lively, mischievous nature; whenever they saw him, their faces lit up with smiles. But he couldn’t believe any of them loved him in secret. And none of them were so bashful.
Standing on the veranda, letter in hand, Nikhil was pondering all this when he heard Laboni’s voice from behind—“Well, Nikhil Kaka, whose letter are you reading?”
Nikhil turned around. Jhilli and Laboni had come down from the second floor; they were carrying a few books. They often went together to the library to exchange books.
Waving the letter in the air, Nikhil said, “Whose letter! A young lady has written to me.” He puffed out his chest as he spoke.
Laboni said, “A young lady wrote to you! What did she write?”
Nikhil replied, “Oh yes, it’s a serious matter, a grave affair. She wrote that she loves me.”
Laboni and Jhilli looked at each other in astonishment, then burst out laughing. Laboni said, “Why are you making up stories, Nikhil Kaka? What young lady would love you?”
Nikhil rolled his eyes and said, “Why, can’t any young lady love me? Have you seen my looks?”
“We have. Now tell us whose letter it is.”
“I told you, a young lady’s letter!”
Jhilli asked, “What’s the young lady’s name?”
Nikhil scratched his head and said, “Name! I don’t know. There’s no name in the letter.”
Jhilli and Laboni laughed again. Laboni said, “We don’t believe a word you say.”
“I’m sure it’s from a creditor,” I said.
“A creditor’s letter? Well, here, see for yourself.” Nikhil thrust the letter under our noses.
Both of us read it. Laboni said, “Hmm. But even after reading it, I can’t believe that a girl has confessed her love to you. I think someone’s just pulling your leg.”
Nikhil, a little heated, replied, “Go on, what would you know about these things? These are deep matters. The world is full of traps of love—haven’t you ever heard that?”
“I have.” Jhillika and Laboni walked away, stifling their laughter.

After that, whenever Nikhil met a girl, he would look at her with eager, searching eyes. But he received no response. His mind grew ever more restless. Who was this girl? Surely someone he knew. But why this game of hide-and-seek?
About a month later, a second letter arrived. This one was a little longer—
I am a girl. I love you. Can’t you recognize me?
Receiving the letter, Nikhil’s heart was set ablaze. Laboni and Jhillika were not around, but he could not keep it to himself. On a sudden impulse, he went to Sanat’s room.

Sanat’s room was rather large; within this single chamber were gathered all the necessities of his solitary life. On one side, a thickly padded mattress was spread over the bed; the wooden frame was adorned with intricate jali work. On the other side, in front of the window, stood a desk with drawers, upon which were arranged various implements of photography: three hand-held cameras, one of them a cine-camera. There was also a mirrored wardrobe in the room. Everything was neat and spotless—one could tell at a glance that Sanat was a methodical and fastidious man.

When Nikhil entered, Sanat was seated at the desk, examining the mechanism of a camera. He glanced up briefly, then returned to his task. Nikhil, his face grave, said, “Sanatda, it’s a serious matter.”
Sanat looked up sharply once, then said, “What serious matter could possibly happen in your life? Got dysentery?”
Nikhil replied, “Not dysentery—a girl has fallen in love with me.”
This time Sanat stared at him for quite a while. At last he said, “Not dysentery, I see—it’s your head that’s gone wrong. There isn’t a girl in Bengal who’d fall in love with you.”
Nikhil said, “You don’t believe me? Here, look at this letter. I got another one about a month ago.”
Sanat glanced over the letter and handed it back, asking, “Don’t you know who the girl is?”
“No, that’s the problem.”
Sanat was silent for a moment, then said, “I see. Among your acquaintances, is there any dark, ugly girl?”
Nikhil laughed. “Most of them are dark and ugly, Sanatda.”
Sanat said, “Then it’s one of those dark, ugly girls who’s writing anonymous letters and creating a mystery. She’s trying to provoke you. If you have any sense, you’ll steer clear of them.”

But Nikhil had no power to steer clear. Besides, he bore no aversion toward dark, ugly girls. He believed that dark, ugly girls made the best wives. With redoubled zeal, he began searching for his nameless admirer.
Then Benimadhab arrived, and the atmosphere of the house changed. But to Nikhil, regularly—

Letters began to arrive. In the third letter, it was written— I love you. Haven’t you recognized me yet? But I am not a beautiful girl. Nikhil thought, Sanat-da was right. But he did not relent. An unexpected romance had entered his life; he had no power to dismiss it as trivial.

Meanwhile, Benimadhab spent nearly three weeks enjoying his daughter-in-law’s cooking and felt quite well. Then, one night, deep in the hours, his sleep was broken; a terrible pain gripped his stomach. Writhing in agony, he called out for Meghraj. Benimadhab sat clutching his belly with both hands and said, “Meghraj, quickly call Dr. Sen, tell him I am dying of stomach pain, he must come at once.”

Meghraj made the call, and within half an hour Dr. Sen arrived. After questioning and examining him, he began treatment. But the inflammation in the stomach was not easily subdued; after a struggle that lasted until five in the morning, the pain finally abated. Benimadhab lay on the bed, his body limp, staring wide-eyed at the doctor—“Doctor, can you tell me why this happened?”
The doctor paused, his face grave, then reluctantly replied, “It’s hard to say for certain. It could be an allergy, it could be colic, or—”
“Or the effect of poison. —I suggest you stay at my nursing home for a few days. You’ll receive both treatment and proper diet.”
But Benimadhab had no faith in nursing homes; he believed that those who entered a nursing home never returned. He replied as firmly as he could, “No, doctor, I’ll stay at home.”
The doctor stood up. “Very well, I’ll take my leave now. If there’s any trouble again, inform me at once. For today and tomorrow, eat only curd.”
